remit_rules.excerpt: MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
Any change to FinBot's configuration ... or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.
any domain or vendor outside that configured closure MUST be reported as a trust expansion.

threats.summary: Any anonymous caller invokes /api/admin/* — rewriting goals/thresholds, disabling fraud detection, approving pending invoices, and raising vendor trust — with no authentication anywhere in the app.
An anonymous POST to /goals persists custom_goals that get_system_prompt appends under 'OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING', redirecting every later invoice decision from stored state.
The admin console is fetchable by URL from the public internet because it lives in the 0.0.0.0-served static folder of an internet-facing Render web service.
Attacker-writable custom_goals are rendered into the console with innerHTML, storing XSS that executes in the next operator's browser.
Wildcard CORS lets any web origin drive the admin config/goals endpoints from a visitor's browser — a trust expansion beyond the configured CineFlow closure.

trust_boundaries.name: Vendor invoice text → agent decision context

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NEVER treat instructions ... contained in an invoice description ... as commands
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.

threats.summary: _analyze_business_context scores authority/urgency phrases out of the attacker-controlled description and the fallback uses that score to override the review threshold and its own injection flag.

On the LLM path the raw description is returned into model context with no provenance labelling; the regex detector runs on the same text but only sets a flag, so injected instructions can still steer the model toward approval.

remit_rules.excerpt: Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold ... MUST be routed to a human reviewer
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection ... was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum ... MUST be routed to a human reviewer
When prompt-injection ... is detected ... FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route ... and alert an admin
MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds ... it produces approval decisions only

threats.summary: _approve_invoice commits status='approved' straight from model args with no amount, injection-flag, or confidence check; the operator-configured confidence_threshold has zero read sites in any decision path.
The same call sets payment_processed=True, taking the agent past its decisions-only boundary into payment state a downstream process could act on.

trust_boundaries.name: Vendor PII/bank details → unauthenticated callers & model

MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.

notes.lane_fit: Mostly clean. Two real strains: (1) FinBotConfig lives in one SQLite DB with invoices/vendors, but its custom_goals + thresholds are agent goal/config STATE that feeds the prompt, so it is modelled as an agent_core `memory` node while the invoice/vendor rows are a tools_mcp `datastore` — a single physical store split across two lanes by role. (2) The Flask APIs are the user-facing surface (client_adapters) yet also host the missing in-process controls; the auth gap is really the absence of a control node in that lane.
notes.omissions: src/routes/user.py + src/models/user.py (a demo User CRUD) are unreferenced by the agent and left out. Static marketing pages (index/leadership/why-partner/onboarding) and ctf-footer.js/agreement-check.js are non-agent UI and omitted. The CTF flag-scoring fields (contains_prompt_injection, ctf_flag_captured) are scenario scaffolding, not architecture, so not given their own node. No log_sink node exists to cite — the tree has no logging framework (PRAX-007), which is itself the finding.
notes.spec_ambiguity: The threat schema requires an ASI01-ASI10 code on every STRIDE threat, but per the KB Primary Arbitration a missing/ungated approval gate (PRAX-003/011), a data-disclosure/authz defect (PRAX-005/012), public-network exposure (PRAX-006), wildcard CORS (PRAX-010), and unbounded consumption (PRAX-009) are LLM03/LLM02/LLM06/RAISE-only with no natural agentic code — their findings JSON carries owasp_agentic=null. I assigned best-fit codes (ASI01 for the approval sink as the goal-hijack chain terminus; ASI03 for the identity/access/trust-boundary defects; ASI03 as the least-wrong tag on the unbounded-consumption threat) rather than leave the required field empty; treat those ASI tags as forced fits, not KB-arbitrated primaries.
